newsitem.title: USA: Ex-hostage Waite still keeps symbolic ticket.
newsitem.headline: Ex-hostage Waite still keeps symbolic ticket.

text.p: Former Lebanon hostage Terry Waite surprised a travel industry awards ceremony on Tuesday by pulling out of his pocket the 9-year-old return portion of a Middle East Airlines ticket he would have used had he not been captured by radical Moslem guerrillas.

Waite, seized by Hezbollah (Party of God) gunmen in January 1987 while on a mission to negotiate the release of Western hostages during the Lebanese civil war, said his luggage had been secured in the British embassy in Beirut until he was freed by his captors in September 1991.

"I went through my luggage and there were papers and just recently I found the return half of the ticket," a jovial Waite told the Business Traveller International magazine annual awards luncheon. "The month of February 1988 was when the return half had to be used by and I was brought home by the Royal Air Force."
"So, MEA if you're hearing, can you still give me a refund?" he said to loud laughter from the audience as he held up the ticket that has become a symbol of his long captivity.
The airline was not among the award recipients, which included Singapore Airlines -- voted by magazine readers for the eighth year running as the Best Airline for International Business Travel.

In the early 1980s, while working for the archbishop of Canterbury, the Anglican Church envoy successfully negotiated the release of several hostages in Iran and Libya before his 1987 mission to Lebanon.
He remained in captivity for 1,760 days, the first four years of which were spent in solitary confinement, much of the time in chains and with few comforts.

Waite, staying at the plush Plaza Hotel in Manhattan where the awards were presented, told the travel executives that when he was asked to write comments in the guest book, he said, "Formerly a guest of Hezbollah, now a guest of the Plaza. It's a very different world."

Waite has dedicated himself to study, writing and humanitarian work since his release and has received several honours, including the Commander of the Order of the British Empire bestowed by Queen Elizabeth.
